source_read: PMC full text PMC7450360 (NIH author manuscript NIHMS1620800) in the reader's own browser tab: abstract, all sections, Tables 1 and 2 (rendered as text), the Figure 1 legend, the collapsed Author information › Contributors statement (read in the DOM), funding, conflict-of-interest statement and reference list. Figure 1 (forest plots) loaded in the page (1033 x 2017 px), but two screenshots of the tab came back blank: figure image not viewable. Step 1 completed before the card was opened.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of direction or causality. On imaging it says findings 'may mix effects', softer than the source's 'likely influencing'. Three phrases are inaccurate as worded and one is incomplete. (1) The simultaneous averages are described as use 'at the same time as cocaine or within a couple of hours'. That is the definition of only one source (Grant & Harford, 1990). The review defines simultaneous use as the same occasion with overlapping consumption or effects (Methods › 2.1, 1st paragraph). The pooled sources asked about co-administration at first use, in a session, ever in one session, use to come down from a cocaine high in the past 30 days, or use together in the past 12 months. Suggested: 'on the same occasion (definitions varied)'. (2) 'Single sources ranged from about a quarter to nearly everyone' holds for alcohol only. Simultaneous cannabis went down to 9.3% and 12.3% (Table 1), 12% in the text. (3) 'None excluded people who drink alcohol or use cannabis' leaves out that two of the 40 imaging studies excluded people who had used cannabis in the past week (3.3; Table 2, rows 9 and 20). (4) Incomplete: '(from the past 30 days to a lifetime)' also covered one urine-test source (Vanek) and one with no stated window (Schwingel). Where a source gave several windows, the shortest was used. No advice on amounts, timing, routes or combinations.
claims.note: Checked against the source, all of these match: 16 estimates = 11 from one PubMed search (January 1990 to June 2017) + 5 secondary analyses of US data sets; 10 US, 3 Canada, 2 Brazil, 1 Denmark; study years 1985-2017; all but one by self-report. Pooled 74% (50-89), 38% (20-60), 77% (62-87), 64% (47-79). I² 97-99%. Text ranges 24-98, 12-76, 37-96, 43-94 against Table 1's 23.5-87, 9.3-76.5, 34.9-96.5 and 43.2-93.7 (the magnitude is right that the fourth agrees). St Louis WTW and STOP (n 463 and 122, all women): to come down, alcohol 23.5% and 36.1%, cannabis 9.3% and 12.3%; past-30-day alcohol 79.5% and 71.3%. 40 imaging studies: 10 excluded alcohol dependence and 10 cannabis dependence (counted in Table 2). Animal studies: 2 of 40 gave alcohol (in utero, and adolescent alcohol before later cocaine), none cannabis. 75% vs 5% and 72.5% (= 29/40) vs 0%. Fisher's exact p recomputed at about 6e-11 and 9e-13 (stated p<0.0001). Tobacco: the authors write that nicotine with other substances, especially alcohol, may be more frequent than cocaine plus alcohol (Discussion, 4th paragraph). No appraisal of the sources is described. Figure 1 was not viewable, and the text does not give how many sources entered each average. Editors' check by DerSimonian-Laird logit pooling of the Table 1 values, using the review's rules (shortest window, powder over crack): it reproduces simultaneous cannabis, 37.9% (19.7-60.3) from 7 sources, and concurrent alcohol, 77.0% (62.1-87.2) from 11 sources, exactly. It gives 70.1% (46.1-86.5) for simultaneous alcohol (8 sources) and 66.5% (49.5-80.1) for concurrent cannabis (8 sources), against the printed 74% and 64%, so the inputs to those two cannot be identified from Table 1. 'Certainty' and 'Status' are not judged here; the 'critically low' rating is from the card (confirmed in step 2).

anchors.locator: 2. Methods › 2.1. Review and meta-analysis of studies with cocaine PSU prevalence, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Definitions: concurrent use = two or more substances within a specified period (e.g. past 30 days). Simultaneous use = on the same occasion with overlapping consumption or effects.

Five secondary data sets: 2014 NSDUH; Women Teaching Women (St Louis outreach, 2000-2006); STOP (St Louis drug courts, 2005-2008); Rx (St Louis outreach, 2008-2010); HealthStreet (north central Florida, past-30-day use). All but NSDUH community-based in defined areas.

PubMed only, human studies, January 1990 to June 2017: 770 records, 134 full texts, 11 included (exclusions by reason, including 1 not in English). Extracted items: author, year, country, sample, PSU rate and measure; no quality or bias appraisal is described. Sample sizes 98 to 36,425. 4 report only simultaneous use, 6 only concurrent, 1 both. Four clinical samples named, including Kedia et al. 2007, which has no Table 1 row.
The 11 literature studies plus 5 secondary analyses = 16 sources. Location, year, sample, demographics and measure summarized.

Meta-analysis in R. Shorter window used where several were reported; powder over crack. I² > 50% = substantial. Chi-square tested at 0.1; random effects when heterogeneity was significant, otherwise fixed. Forest plot.

anchors.locator: 3. Results › 3.1.1. Review of studies including PSU prevalence, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Ranges among people who use cocaine as stated in the text: simultaneous alcohol 24-98%, simultaneous cannabis 12-76%, concurrent alcohol 37-96%, concurrent cannabis 43-94%. 10 US, 3 Canada, 2 Brazil, 1 Denmark; study period 1985-2017; mean ages 22-44. One source by medical records and urine tests (Vanek), the rest by self-report. Populations from rural not-in-treatment to treatment-seeking, students, rave attendees, bodybuilders, people using hallucinogens or prescription drugs.

Simultaneous measures differed: same time or within a couple of hours (Grant & Harford); co-administration (Barrett 2005); using alcohol or cannabis to come down from a cocaine high (WTW, STOP). Concurrent windows: mostly 30 days, also 6 months (Booth), past year (Hedden), lifetime (Guindalini), both positive in a urine test (Vanek).
I² 97% to 99%; chi-square p<0.01 in all four analyses; random effects used.
Pooled prevalence among people who use cocaine: simultaneous alcohol 74% (95% CI 50-89), simultaneous cannabis 38% (20-60), concurrent alcohol 77% (62-87), concurrent cannabis 64% (47-79).

Figure image not viewable (two blank screenshots), so the number of sources and weights per estimate could not be read. Editors' DerSimonian-Laird logit check from Table 1: 37.9% (19.7-60.3) from 7 sources and 77.0% (62.1-87.2) from 11 match the printed estimates. Simultaneous alcohol (8 sources) gives 70.1% (46.1-86.5) and concurrent cannabis (8) gives 66.5% (49.5-80.1), which do not match.

Among people who use cocaine, Table 1 values run: simultaneous alcohol 23.5% (WTW) to 87% (Licht); simultaneous cannabis 9.3% (WTW) to 76.5% (Barrett 2005); concurrent alcohol 34.9% (Vanek, urine) to 96.5% (Grant & Harford); concurrent cannabis 43.2% (WTW) to 93.7% (Guindalini, lifetime). Three of these differ from the text's ranges.

anchors.locator: Table 1, rows 13 (Women Teaching Women) and 14 (Sisters Teaching Options for Prevention)
anchors.extracted: St Louis, 100% women, people who used cocaine in the past 30 days (n=463 community; n=122 drug court). Used alcohol to come down from a cocaine high in the past 30 days: 23.5% and 36.1%; cannabis: 9.3% and 12.3%. Past-30-day alcohol: 79.5% and 71.3%; cannabis: 43.2% and 46.7%.

anchors.locator: 2. Methods › 2.3. Exploratory analysis of frequency of inclusion of PSU in human or animal cocaine studies, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Human: PubMed 'fMRI AND cocaine', the 40 most recent papers as of 1 January 2018 with cocaine use as the exposure and a neuroimaging/fMRI outcome. Animal: 'cocaine' filtered to other animals, read in reverse chronological order from 1 January 2018; in vivo cocaine in mammals with a neurobiological or behavioural outcome.

anchors.locator: 3.3. Exploratory analysis of the frequency of PSU in human and preclinical studies, 1st paragraph; Table 2
anchors.extracted: No human study excluded alcohol or cannabis users; two excluded past-week cannabis users. Dependence was mostly an exclusion criterion for the controls. 10 of 40 excluded alcohol dependence and 10 cannabis dependence (Table 2 count agrees). Animal: 2 of 40 gave alcohol and cocaine (in utero alcohol; adolescent alcohol before later cocaine), none gave cannabis. 75% vs 5% and 72.5% (29/40) vs 0%, Fisher's exact p<0.0001 (recomputed at about 6e-11 and 9e-13). The authors add that excluding PSU is valid for some animal questions.

Few studies focus on cocaine PSU patterns. Several rates had to be calculated by the authors (Booth, Hedden, Vanek). Only Grant & Harford separated concurrent from simultaneous use. Heterogeneity is high, possibly from sampling and measurement.
Nicotine with other substances, particularly alcohol, may be more frequent than cocaine with alcohol but is not consistently recorded in studies of illicit drug use. Not part of the pooled estimates.

key_findings.correction: The card's arithmetic on n=21,970 is right: 48.7% of 36,425 = 17,739 is fewer than 21,970.

Two precision points. 'Male volunteers' comes from the cited paper's title in the reference list (Lukas et al., 1994), not from the review's text. The review says the neurobiological effects of long-term cocaethylene administration have not been assessed (3.2.1, 2nd paragraph), which is narrower than 'the long-term effects of cocaethylene have not been studied'.

Accurate for the pretreatment designs, but it leaves out the second phase of Czoty (2015) in the same paragraph. With daily alcohol access after cocaine sessions, 5 of 6 monkeys self-administered cocaine doses that had not been reinforcing before, and those doses stopped being self-administered when alcohol access ended. It also leaves out that alcohol pretreatment increased nomifensine self-administration in Aspen & Winger's monkeys. These results are what the review's dopamine-agonist conclusion rests on.

Minor: the polysubstance groups of Pennington et al. (2015) and Schmidt et al. (2017) had alcohol use disorder plus dependence on another drug (76% and 75% cocaine), not all cocaine-and-alcohol dependence.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in step 1. The pooled figures can be partly checked: DerSimonian-Laird logit pooling of Table 1 values reproduces simultaneous cannabis (7 sources) and concurrent alcohol (11 sources) exactly, but not simultaneous alcohol (70.1%, 46.1-86.5, from 8) or concurrent cannabis (66.5%, 49.5-80.1, from 8). Unconfirmed lead for the editor: using HealthStreet's alcohol-and-cannabis figure (43.7%) in place of its cannabis figure (61.5%) gives 64.5% (47.0-78.8).
Methods › 2.1, 3rd paragraph names Kedia among four clinical samples; Table 1 has no Kedia row; Hedden 2009 (row 6) carries n=36,425, Kedia's figure in the Introduction.
The cited title in the review's reference list confirms the study was about myocardial steatosis by 1H MR spectroscopy (Table 2, row 25).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: several critical items not met (no protocol, PubMed only, no list of exclusions, no appraisal, no publication-bias assessment). The item 5 note is borne out by the Contributors statement in the collapsed Author information: one author ran the epidemiology search and the meta-analysis.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial, for the abstract's bare pooled figures, the untested alcohol-vs-cannabis comparison, the causal reading of cross-sectional imaging, and the unequal human-vs-animal counting. One correction to the card's reasoning: the review's statement that combined alcohol increases the reinforcing qualities of dopamine agonists is not contradicted by its cited monkey studies. It draws on the nomifensine increase and Czoty's concurrent-access phase (see key finding 10). It remains a generalization from a handful of monkeys.

missed: 3.3, 1st paragraph: in most of the 40 imaging studies, alcohol or cannabis dependence was an exclusion criterion for the control subjects only, so the cocaine groups and their controls differed in alcohol and cannabis dependence. This strengthens the point that imaging findings may mix effects.
3.3, 1st paragraph: the authors add that excluding polysubstance use is valid for some animal experiments; their point is that it is rarely considered.
Editors' reconstruction of the pooled estimates from Table 1 (see reporting issue 0): two of four reproduce exactly; the inputs to simultaneous alcohol and concurrent cannabis cannot be identified.
